item.title: VPN provider built a script to block Microsoft's hidden GDID tracking on Windows — Windscribe's "deGDID" erases existing identifiers and blocks new ones from being created
item.description: Score: 5.45 A VPN provider named Windscribe has released an open-source script called "deGDID" designed to block Microsoft's Global Device Identifier (GDID) tracking on Windows PCs. The script operates by purging cached GDID keys from the registry and modifying Access Control Lists to prevent the operating system from re-minting new identifiers. While effective at blocking new tracking, the process can cause core Microsoft cloud services to malfunction, and the script is only functional on unmanaged systems with administrative access. item.content:encoded: Last month, we covered a federal criminal case in which Microsoft's Global Device Identifier (GDID) helped the FBI catch an alleged hacker. Despite the noble cause, the implications of a persistent tracker built into Windows became difficult to ignore, and it was enough of a tipping point to convince Windscribe to do something about it. The VPN company has created an open-source project and script called "deGDID" that aims to strip GDID off your PC — but does so at the cost of breaking some Microsoft cloud services. You can find the script on GitHub and run it via PowerShell with admin privileges. It's completely free and works in a very straightforward manner. There are three main execution flags that dictate how deGDID operates: –Status, which is read-only and tells you if a GDID is active on your rig; –Status –Redact, which generates logs with the GDID redacted so users can share diagnostic data more confidently; and –Protect, which completely wipes the GDID and prevents the creation of new ones. A fourth flag, –Unprotect, allows you to reverse the script in case you need to revert back to the default state. But –Protect is the one worth discussing. First, the script looks for server-issued GDID keys in the registry, where they remain cached, and purges them all. This is something you can do manually as well. In fact, Windscribe tried it on a virtual machine, but the GDID keys are silently re-minted in the background upon a reboot or whenever Windows contacts Microsoft servers again. To close this loop, the script then modifies the ACLs (Access Control Lists) and registry permissions to prevent the OS from fetching and subsequently trying to remint the GDID keys. It puts up a firewall against the internal DeviceAdd endpoint, which completely cuts off Microsoft identity services from even seeing this as a registered Windows PC. This one-two punch completes the process, and the existing GDID keys are not only wiped, but the possibility of new ones being created is put to bed as well. Keep in mind that old keys that are already server-side cannot be removed; Microsoft has access to them indefinitely. This script also only works on unmanaged systems with admin accounts. If you're part of an organization or domain, deGDID will refuse to run. More importantly, though, since it blocks Microsoft's DeviceAdd pipeline, some core Windows services will break because they'll fail to authenticate your Microsoft account. The reason deGDID is even needed in the first place is that Windows has no native toggle to turn off GDID. It exists as a permanent device ID that can track you without your consent. It works across IP addresses since it sits beneath the layer where VPNs operate, so no amount of network tunneling can obfuscate it. This can explain why Windscribe was compelled to create deGDID — to combat a potentially invasive system that has the power to wreak havoc in the wrong hands. We tried the script on a Windows 11 computer, and it worked as intended. Running the –Status flag showed multiple cached GDIDs that were then removed by the –Protect flag, and a new GDID didn't show up even after restarting. As expected, some Microsoft apps freaked out and returned connection errors. Account verification through login.live.com was also blocked across all browsers, though login.microsoftonline.com still worked. Online games and other apps continued to behave normally as well. Windscribe says deGDID is a research project, and it will continue to evolve as more information about how GDID works is uncovered. For now, the fact that it can make core Microsoft services and features fail might be too much of a tradeoff for some. The script also doesn't promise to kill every GDID instance, and Microsoft already has your previous keys, so this is certainly not an ideal solution — but it's a good start to the fight against hidden trackers. item.content:encoded: What's the difference between the Apple Pencil USB-C Vs Pro? And which one will work with your iPad? Since its introduction in 2015, the Apple Pencil has grown into an indispensable gadget for its users. Die-hard fans will tell you that the stylus has revolutionized how they use their tablet, expanding the creative possibilities and maximizing their iPad experience. With four generations of the product on the market, however, it's understandable that customers have some reservations about finding the Apple Pencil that is right for them. Deciphering the Apple Pencil lineup can be tough. One reason for the difficulty is that Apple sells four generations of styluses whose differences aren't very visually apparent. For instance, the two most recent iterations, the Apple Pencil Pro and Apple Pencil (USB-C), sport similar dimensions. Moreover, both styluses look fairly similar beyond the latter's USB-C charging port. From a functionality perspective, both offer a high-end stylus experience, delivering "pixel-perfect precision" with low latency rates. Add a hover feature that allows you to preview your stylus' markings and tilt sensitivity that enables shading and other visual effects, and both Apple Pencils deliver a polished experience capable of taking your iPad usage to new heights. With that said, which generation of Apple Pencil you choose can have a major effect on your experience. Although both models are capable styluses, the Apple Pencil Pro offers several feature upgrades that may be worth considering. Of course, these enhancements come at a price. As it stands, the Apple Pencil Pro is $50 more expensive than its Apple Pencil (USB-C) counterpart, with models retailing for $129 and $79, respectively. Whether its enhanced features are worth the extra cash will likely depend on your intended usage. If you are a student who just needs the stylus to take notes in class, then the standard Apple Pencil will likely fulfill most of your needs. But artists and creatives looking for an Apple Pencil that delivers a greater sense of control may find Apple Pencil Pro to be well worth the cash. Which you choose will likely depend on your budget, iPad model and daily usage. And if it weren't confusing enough, EU regulations may force Apple to institute a refreshed lineup featuring replaceable batteries. For now, however, let's compare the latest models to decide if upgrading to an Apple Pencil Pro is right for you. The Apple Pencil Pro brings a host of new features, but are they worth it? The Apple Pencil Pro enables you to enjoy several advanced features that may enhance your stylistic experience. One example is the stylus' heightened pressure sensitivity, which allows you to adjust the thickness and darkness of lines based on the pressure you place on the pen while you write. Another feature, dubbed "Barrel Roll," enables you to shift the orientation of your brush tools. By simply rotating the barrel while you draw, the pen will mimic the changing orientation of a paintbrush. This feature uses a gyroscope to give you greater control over your pen's markings. Another useful add-on is the pencil's squeeze functions. With the Apple Pencil Pro, users can switch between creative tools by squeezing the pen's body. This action opens up a palette, allowing users to seamlessly switch between colors, line weights and brushes. You can also make these changes by utilizing the pen's double-tap feature, in which tapping its base twice in quick succession moves you between mediums, such as switching from a pen to an eraser and back again. Many of these features are supported by the pen's haptic feedback system, which issues slight pulses through the pen's body to confirm its execution of a squeeze or double tap. In addition to these creative features, the Apple Pencil Pro adds several elements that make using the pencil more convenient. For instance, users can now charge their Apple Pencil wirelessly whenever they magnetically attach it to their tablet's side. This means that you won't have to worry about plugging in another gadget every evening. Instead, the Apple Pencil Pro is stored and charged the same way, removing yet another barrier between you and your creations. Another logistical change is that your Apple Pencil Pro can now integrate with your Find My app, allowing you to easily find your stylus if you misplace it. Apple also enables you to engrave your Apple Pencil Pro for free, further preventing any questions of mistaken identity. No word if the engineering team in Cupertino has figured out how to stop their products from hiding out in the creases of your couch cushion. Is your Apple Pencil compatible? Perhaps the most important question to ask yourself when purchasing an Apple Pencil is: What products do I plan on using it with? Because the Apple Pencil Pro is a relatively new product, it is only compatible with a select group of iPads. Moreover, consumers who are using older iPads may need to opt for even older Apple Pencil models than the Apple Pencil USB-C. As it stands, the Apple Pencil Pro is compatible with the following iPad models: - iPad Pro 13-inch (M4, M5) - iPad Pro 11-inch (M4, M5) - iPad Air 13-inch (M2, M3, M4) - iPad Air 11-inch (M2, M3, M4) - iPad mini (A17 Pro) Consumers who would rather opt for the Apple Pencil (USB-C) can use their product on a wider array of iPads. The full list of tablets compatible with the Apple Pencil (USB-C) includes: - iPad Pro 13-inch (M4, M5) - iPad Pro 12.9-inch (3rd, 4th, 5th, 6th generations) - iPad Pro 11-inch (M4, M5) - iPad Pro 11-inch (1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th generations) - iPad Air 13-inch (M2, M3, M4) - iPad Air 11-inch (M2, M3, M4) - iPad Air (4th, 5th generations) - iPad (A16) - iPad (10th generation) - iPad mini (A17 Pro) - iPad mini (6th generation) If you're using an older version of Apple's flagship tablet, you can visit the guide on Apple's support page to find the Apple Pencil that is right for you. There, you can gauge the compatibility of all four Apple Pencil models.

item.content:encoded: Apple filed a lawsuit against OpenAI in July, alleging that the latter stole trade secrets through former Apple employees. The startup has finally publicly responded to the lawsuit today, posting a blog post on its website titled, “Apple is getting this wrong.” “Apple is one of the greatest companies of all time, and built a reputation for obsessing over the smallest details. This careless, aggressive and oddly personal lawsuit sadly doesn’t live up to that reputation,” the company said in its blog post. It also added, “Apple’s request for a preliminary injunction is both based on false information and completely unnecessary because we do not have, nor want, any of their trade secrets.” The case names OpenAI technical staff Chang Liu, chief hardware officer Tang Tan, OpenAI, and io Products as defendants. Liu worked as a senior electrical engineer at Apple, while Tan was its former vice president of product design for the iPhone, AirPods, and the Apple Watch. Interestingly, io Products, which was acquired by OpenAI last year, was founded by Tan alongside former Apple Chief Design Officer Jony Ive and other former Apple heavyweights. The tech giant requested a preliminary injunction to stop the accused from accessing, acquiring, using, or disclosing the alleged stolen trade secrets. Cupertino said in its filing, “Apple will be irreparably harmed absent a preliminary injunction.” OpenAI publicly responded to this legal request through its blog post, pointing out that many of its allegations were actually based on miscommunications and false information, and that this move is completely unnecessary. But whether what the AI tech giant claims is true or not, its research and operations on consumer hardware would likely be impaired if the judge grants Apple’s request. Although OpenAI’s primary product is ChatGPT and its other LLM-powered services, it’s been rumored that it’s also working on AI-powered hardware. Its first product is expected to be some sort of portable smart speaker with built-in cameras and sensors. Although this isn’t an iPhone replacement, like the botched Humane AI Pin, some experts say this move threatens Apple’s standing as the biggest consumer electronics company on the planet. This is especially true as it still lags behind other tech giants when it comes to artificial intelligence, even though AI enthusiasts love using Apple silicon with its Unified Memory architecture. Apple’s preliminary injunction is just the opening stages of what might be an epic showdown between two tech giants. It will likely take months (or even years) before this case reaches a judgment or a settlement, meaning a preliminary injunction will definitely have a massive impact on OpenAI’s hardware dreams. item.title: Hank Green found the AI problem that YouTube labels can’t catch
item.description: Score: 5.49 The article critiques YouTube's AI disclosure policy, arguing that its guidelines create confusing and inconsistent boundaries for content creators. The author points out that while some AI uses require mandatory disclosure, other significant uses, such as idea generation, scripting, and voice cloning, do not, creating potential gaps, especially for complex geopolitical content. The piece concludes by contrasting AI-assisted creation with human-led processes, suggesting AI imparts a specific, potentially limiting, logic to projects. item.content:encoded: YouTube currently requires that content creators let viewers know “when they use AI to meaningfully alter or generate photorealistic content.” The policy draws some strange boundaries. It applies to “AI-generated music” (not photorealistic) but not to “riding a unicorn through a fantastical world” (this could be photorealistic, though it is not plausible). YouTube then summarizes the policy in a different way: “Realistic AI content and meaningful changes require disclosure, while non-realistic or minor edits don’t.” But AI uses that require no disclosure can include everything from “idea generation” up through “production assistance, like using generative AI tools to create or improve a video outline, script, thumbnail, title, or infographic.” Creators are free to clone their own voices for voiceovers. They can also use “AI-generated or altered animation of a missile in a fully animated video.” This results in some odd scenarios. A thrilling 10-second video that shows me riding my AI-generated steed through the horse-killing-fart swamps of Soylentius IV? No disclosure, even though the entire thing is AI-generated. But when I add an AI-crafted lute ballad about the grave dangers I faced in those swamps? Mandatory disclosure. The policy gap becomes more consequential when you imagine a 30-minute video attempting to sway people’s views on geopolitics. AI could generate the premise, do the research, and write the outline. My own AI-cloned voice model could read the AI-drafted script. I could even use AI-generated missile animations. Must I disclose the rampant AI use that drove this entire project? Apparently not. But having an AI help in these ways imparts a certain feel and logic to projects, even if the final result is not fully “AI-generated.” Humans approaching topics without AI might find sources through quite different paths, and they might have to read and process more material to get there, giving them a different kind of understanding. They might also note very different things as important, thus creating different outlines of the same material. They might pepper a script with jokes or digressions not usually suggested by an AI. And they might read a script aloud in a more natural way.

Pros - +Four Included Fans - +Great normalized cooling performance on the CPU - +Tiered ARGB PSU Shroud - +Showcase space Cons - -Slightly higher GPU temperatures - -Non-color-matched PSU shroud is polarizing Why you can trust Tom's Hardware We first spotted Montech's TG3 case at Computex earlier this year. This panoramic mid-tower chassis offers a full view inside through the smoked side and front panel glass, and features a tiered bottom layout and an ARGB lighting strip around the raised power supply chamber. While the side intake isn’t a boon for high airflow, the case performed well in our testing with our power-hungry components, at least with the CPU, offering some of the best air-cooled temperatures using our new test hardware. Priced at $59.90 including four fans (or technically two, as one is a full-frame 360mm), it offers a great value in the budget mid-tower space. Inside, the TG3 comes with preinstalled unibody reverse fans (3x120mm) on the side and a single 120mm fan on the rear for factory-provided airflow. Up top, there’s room for three more 120mm fans / a 360mm radiator, too. The chassis supports motherboards from ATX down to Mini-ITX, and even handles rear-connect motherboards. The TG3 supports huge graphics cards, and even vertical GPU mounting (with a kit sold separately). The power supply sits in its own tiered chamber, silver in color, adding dimensional depth to the interior. The chamber sports a frosted RGB strip that runs along the top edge and casts a nice glow on your components inside the chassis. At the front of the case, on the bottom, is showcase space to show off a figure, or whatever you want that fits, or it’s wasted space. Externally, this is a simple design, with two panes of lightly tinted glass on the front and side, showing off your internals. It comes in black and white, with the latter using a color-matched PSU chamber, unlike our black model. The IO panel runs along the bottom edge and offers two Type-A ports, a single Type-C port, along with power and RGB mode buttons. Overall, it’s a good-looking chassis, especially for the sub-$60 price point. The TG3 sits on four integrated raised feet, with rubber pads that slightly lift the case for better airflow. ▶️ Internal Features Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox. Inside the chassis, there’s quite a bit of space because of the side (not front) fans, which give you an extra couple of inches to play with up front. Montech decided to use the extra space at the bottom, between the PSU shroud and the front glass panel, as a stage for you to put something there to show off. Perhaps a Gundam figure, your waifu, or any other cool model or trophy to personalize the space. Otherwise, it’s just space that could have been better utilized, maybe as a sloped shroud directing cooled air up towards the GPU. The motherboard panel supports up to ATX boards, with mounting points for Mini-ITX and MicroATX form factors. The best fit is for sure ATX and MicroATX, as that’s where all the cable management holes line up. It also supports rear-connect motherboards (BTF, Project Zero, Stealth) for that ultra-clean, wire-free aesthetic. There’s plenty of room to route the cables through the grommets. Speaking of grommets, I like when cases use these as it further hides the wires. However, they almost always come out of their spaces easily, including on the TG3. I wish they were glued in so you didn’t have to push them back in after you’re doing cable routing. As you can see, the chassis comes with a total of four 120mm fans, with three on the side as intake and one rear exhaust. The fans hail from Montech's GF U line, specifically the unibody GF360 U Rev, and a GF120 U for the rear. Both 25mm-thick fans have ARGB blades and spin at 800-1,600 RPM on Hydrodynamic bearings. Montech lists airflow up to 73.1 CFM and static pressure around 1.71 mmH2O. That's not a lot of static pressure, but it doesn’t need to be, since they are case fans with relatively low resistance. Montech says it does so at a whisper-quiet 25.3 dBA. And while we can’t fully verify the fan's specs, the case was quiet out of the box during our full-load tests. The top of the case pops off from below, by more of those ball-and-socket capture mechanisms. From the inside, you can mount three 120 or 140mm fans/radiators, with plenty of room for a standard-thickness radiator and fans. Outside of that, there’s nothing special in this area. The next internal feature worth calling out is the PSU shroud. While it might sound boring, there’s actually a lot going on here. First, in the black chassis, the shroud is gray and doesn’t match. This was an intentional design choice to make it stand out in the black colorway, but personally, I’m not sold on it and would like to see it all in black. That said, the white TG3 does have it matching in white. Running along the edge is a frosted RGB strip that adds a bit more ‘native’ bling to the case. Finally, on top of the chamber there is room for two additional 120mm fans to cool the graphics card directly, but using those removes at least one PCIe expansion slot. Flipping the case around to the back side and opening it up, we get a better shot of the unibody GF360 U fan mounting. Note that you have some vertical flexibility in mounting location (what you see is how it arrived). There isn’t a ton of space for stashing cables behind the motherboard panel, but enough, and Montech includes two Velcro ties for a cleaner look. item.content:encoded: Apple and OpenAI are heading to court in a clash of two of the world's largest and most well-funded companies. With teams of lawyers and bottomless pockets to fund them, these two industry titans are squaring off over claims of theft of trade secrets. Apple is asking the courts to block its former employees from revealing information to their new employer and limit OpenAI's development of an AI device based on Apple technology. Unsurprisingly, OpenAI denies any wrongdoing and is asking the judge not to disrupt its business activities. "Apple's getting this wrong" is the name of the blog post OpenAI posted in response to Apple's lawsuit. Although it begins by calling Apple one of the greatest companies of all time, it goes on to call the legal action "sad," suggests Apple mixed up Asian employee names, and doesn't want its trade secrets anyway. OpenAI went on to publish text message chains and email correspondence, suggesting it's keen to be tried in the court of public opinion more than any other setting. Hey, that's mine! Apple alleges that as many as 13 of its former employees may have passed along sensitive trade secrets to OpenAI, including sharing details of unannounced products and sharing screenshots of confidential Apple documents. This is an expansion of its original claims from July, when it alleged two former employees may have shared confidential information with OpenAI. It has now filed a concurrent motion seeking expedited discovery, demanded that two former employees, Chang Liu and Tang Yew Tan, sit for depositions, as well as key OpenAI employees and representatives of OpenAI's hardware division, io Products. Apple is also asking for a preliminary injunction, which would bar former employees from accessing, acquiring, or disclosing any confidential information about the company as the case proceeds. Considering a case of this magnitude, between two companies with effectively infinite money to spend protecting themselves, that could take months or years to resolve, that preliminary injunction is key and could mean the lawsuit does enough damage to be effective for Apple's goals. Regardless, OpenAI is in full revolt over the process and has posted not only a damning denial of all claims, but some evidence it feels exonerates its position, too. Getting ahead of the competition The cynical argument for this lawsuit is that it means the two companies are battling it out in a courtroom instead of in the consumer retail space. Apple is first and foremost a consumer device company, and to date, OpenAI hasn't competed there. But it's planning to, and its various hires from Apple and elsewhere, including buying up Jony Ive's hardware company, suggest it's going to release something with the kind of smart consumer focus that is typically Apple's bread and butter. Apple might have been a little late to the AI game, but that's played to its advantage. But if OpenAI were to use its strong mindshare, deep pockets, and advanced AI model design and inferencing compute base to offer something targeting mainstream consumers, it's stepping on Apple's toes. This lawsuit could be a way to stop that in its tracks. That's not to say the lawsuit may not have merit. The entire AI industry has used aggressively expensive hiring practices to try to get ahead. Meta spent $15 billion on getting Alexandr Wang and ScaleAI's data, and AI companies are reportedly hounding promising students years ahead of graduation to lock them into future contracts. If you're building a smart consumer device, though? Grabbing ex- or even current Apple employees wouldn't be a bad way to do it. Especially if they brought along information on unannounced Apple products that may or may not be related to an AI consumer device. First to market matters, too. Although Apple hasn't shown any AI-first standalone devices yet, if it were planning to, slowing OpenAI down with these injunctions might be enough to let it catch up or even get ahead. Clock's ticking For now, the lawsuit is very much he-said, she-said. Both companies have enough money and resources to make this fight messy, but what they don't necessarily have is time. Especially OpenAI. It's on the hook for hundreds of billions in compute investment, has just cut the price of some of its models, and has yet to post anything close to a profitable quarter. Apple isn't quite so constrained, but is also seeing its traditional consumer base eaten by rapidly appreciating electronics costs. Apple already sells its products at a premium. But what can it do if prices for components push its products out of the luxury affordable into the truly unaffordable? That may not happen, but it's a future it has to consider as AI, and the money spent on its promised future continues to have an outsized impact on global economies. The outcome of this lawsuit is likely to leave a mark, too. Jon Martindale is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. For the past 20 years, he's been writing about PC components, emerging technologies, and the latest software advances. His deep and broad journalistic experience gives him unique insights into the most exciting technology trends of today and tomorrow.

item.content:encoded: For most of its existence, the Tesla Supercharger network was both the automaker’s crown jewel and a walled garden. Tightly integrated to work only with Tesla electric vehicles, the DC fast-charging experience for Tesla customers was painless in ways that EV drivers dependent on CCS1 chargers operated by a patchwork of networks could only dream of. Then, in 2023, Tesla began opening up the network to other EVs. Ford was the first to sign a deal, and by the following year, the CCS1 plug, which was the de facto non-Tesla standard, was living on borrowed time. But it’s not just other automakers that are adopting the J3400 standard, better known as NACS. Manufacturers of DC fast charging equipment can also license Tesla’s Supercharger design. In fact, the first license-built Superchargers were deployed in the UK in 2024. And today we learned that’s what EVgo will be doing here in the US. It says it will start deploying EVgo-made Tesla V4 Superchargers onto its network later this fall. The DC chargers can deliver up to 500 kW (operating at up to 1,000 V) and support both NACS and CCS1 plugs. And because they’re Tesla Superchargers built under license, the EVgo units will appear in Tesla’s in-car navigation app and be included when a Tesla driver uses their onboard route planner. The hardware will be owned and operated by EVgo, which will also “manage activities such as site host engagement, utility interconnection, and price management at EVgo Supercharger sites,” the company told Ars.

item.content:encoded: Why smartphone makers stopped using removable batteries, and why they're making a comeback The ability to replace my phone's battery? Yes, please. There was a time when replacing a phone's battery was as easy as popping the back cover off and lifting the battery from its slot with your fingernail. While you can still find a few devices with easily replaceable batteries these days, the design isn't anywhere near mainstream anymore. They're pretty much obsolete, and there are many reasons why they are, which we'll get to later. But a soon-to-be-implemented European Union regulation could bring some form of them back in the near future. Are there still any smartphones with removable batteries? One model you can still get in 2026 is the Samsung Galaxy XCover 7 Pro, a military-grade rugged phone with an easily swappable 4,350mAh battery. It was built for tough environments, and the idea is that you can replace its battery if you lose power while hiking or mountain climbing. Another model you can get today with an easily replaceable battery is the Fairphone 6. It's built a bit differently than the earlier models in the series, which come with back covers you can easily take off. It uses components that make it slimmer, but that also means its battery is held in place with five screws. The battery is still pretty easy to replace, but it takes a bit more effort now. So why aren't phones with swappable batteries a thing anymore? It's a combination of several factors, including people's preference for thinner designs. Phones with removable batteries require certain parts and mechanisms, like screws and clips, that typically make them thicker. Companies also have more freedom to squeeze components into a thinner body in creative ways if they don't have to think about how to position a battery slot so that it's easily accessible. In addition, people now prefer premium materials like glass and aluminum for their handhelds. Glass, especially, may be too fragile for a removable back panel. The Fairphone 6's body and back panel are made of plastic. The Galaxy XCover 7 Pro's is, as well — it's even pretty flexible. Samsung's Galaxy S5, another model with a removable battery released in 2014, also has a plastic chassis. Most modern phones have sealed bodies to protect them from dust and water, as well. The iPhone 17 series, for instance, has an IP68 water and dust resistance rating and can remain submerged in 19-foot-deep water for 30 minutes. Removable back covers could pop out when dropped or mishandled, making phones more vulnerable to water and dust. However, it's not entirely impossible for a phone to have a removable back cover and battery and still be water-resistant: The Samsung Galaxy XCover 7 Pro, for example, has an IP68 rating. Samsung told GSM Arena that it put seals on different parts of the phone, such as the camera, to protect its components. The phone's back cover also has gaskets that align with the SIM and the battery slots to make sure they're protected. Finally, batteries that are easy to remove and replace could make people hold on to their devices longer instead of upgrading more frequently. And let's just say companies wouldn't love that. Will phones in 2027 have replaceable batteries? Starting in February 2027, a new law will come into force in the European Union. The law, which has been years in the making, requires companies to sell phones and tablets with removable batteries in the bloc. It's meant to extend the lifespan of devices and reduce waste, as well as make it easier to get raw materials like lithium and cobalt from old batteries. Because companies are less likely to release a special version just for the EU than to simply adopt a new universal design, the rest of us could be getting removable batteries, as well. The best example of this is the iPhone, which now comes with a USB-C port instead of the Lightning port, because of an EU regulation that made USB-C the common charging standard in the region. Despite the upcoming rule, you still probably won't see a lot of phones with back covers and batteries you can easily pry off with your nails. According to the language in the regulation, a battery is "considered to be removable by the end-user" if it can be removed with commercially available tools like screwdrivers. They must not require specialized tools, "unless they are provided free of charge," and they can't use adhesives that would need heating or solvents to remove. That means phones could still have back covers and batteries secured by screws, and companies could just ship them off with special tools if they use anything that can't be removed by standard screwdrivers. However, there is a carveout in the rules that could mean Apple doesn't have to redesign the iPhone. It states that companies can just provide replacement batteries to professional repairers (not end users) if their devices meet certain requirements. First, the model's battery must have a remaining capacity of at least 83 percent in a fully charged state after 500 charge cycles. After 1,000 charge cycles, the device's battery health must be at least 80 percent. Finally, the device must have an IP67 rating, at least, which means it's dust-tight and can survive temporary immersion in water. On its support page, Apple says the batteries of iPhones 15 and newer were designed "to retain 80 percent of their original capacity at 1,000 complete charge cycles under ideal conditions." And as we mentioned earlier, the iPhone 17 series has a rating of IP68. Of course, devices other than the iPhone could be exempted, as well, if they meet those requirements. In other words, you will likely see a bunch of new phones starting next year with batteries that are relatively easy to replace, but companies may not have to drastically change the designs of their more expensive models.

item.content:encoded: As the United States’ five-month-old war with Iran continues to evolve, Tehran’s ability to continue punishing the United States and its allies has come as a surprise to many strategists and analysts. For months, the United States and Israel have intermittently pummeled the country with air strikes, decapitating much of its senior leadership. Yet Iran and its regional allies have proved remarkably dogged: Hezbollah remains a threat despite Israel’s blistering campaign in southern Lebanon, Iran-backed Iraqi militias have attacked Gulf oil and gas infrastructure, and the Houthis in Yemen have restarted their campaign against commercial ships in the Red Sea. In fact, the resilience of both the Islamic Republic and its partners despite years of apparent setbacks points to an underlying flaw in the thinking that led to the conflict. In launching the campaign against Iran in late February, the United States and Israel were drawing on a theory pushed by American regime-change advocates and Israeli strategists for years: by targeting the Islamic Republic’s economy, its leadership, weapons facilities, and central supply lines with military force and economic sanctions, Washington could fatally undermine the Iranian regime. In doing so, it would also deal a decisive blow to the regime’s allies. Sever the head of the octopus in Tehran, the theory went, and the axis groups—the octopus’s many arms—would shrivel and die, too. Two decades ago, a military campaign motivated by the so-called octopus doctrine might have worked. At that point, the relationship between Iran and its allies was less complex, with arms, technology, and know-how all routed through Tehran. But the axis is no longer organized as a simple system with easily identifiable points of failure. Today, it more closely resembles a densely interconnected, self-reproducing web, in which knowledge, resources, and even decision-making can be pooled in many different places at the same time. When a leader is killed, a manufacturing site or warehouse is bombed, or a supply line is cut off, the various groups that are involved adapt, quickly replacing the slain leader, filling in technical knowledge gaps needed to build weapons, and reconstituting supply lines via alternative routes. It is this increasingly sophisticated and flexible structure that has allowed Iran’s allies to adapt in the years since Hamas’s October 7 attacks. Even after Israel’s devastation of Hamas and Hezbollah during the war in Gaza and the collapse of the Assad regime in Syria—and even after the massive U.S.-Israeli air campaign against Iran this spring—the axis has remained largely intact. As a result, Washington can no longer fall back on its go-to toolkit of escalating political pressure, sanctions, and military strikes. Outright defeat of Iran and the axis groups is likely out of reach, but limiting the threat they pose is still possible. Doing so will require the United States to develop a more comprehensive regional strategy aimed at addressing the complex international military, financial, and knowledge networks that now sustains Iranian power. Washington must now consider containing and potentially striking deals with Iran and its most powerful nonstate allies. And it must do whatever is necessary to limit the spread of the low-cost technology employed in the weapons systems designed by Iran and used by the axis, including engaging with China. This approach may not be satisfying to those American leaders who demand a resounding victory in the Middle East. But it stands a much better chance of success than the current strategy of attacking Iran over and over again and hoping that the Islamic Republic and its network of allies will eventually collapse. UPSKILLING THE AXIS Twenty years ago, the groups now known as the “axis of resistance” were mostly local insurgents using the tactics and technology of twentieth-century guerrillas. Under Iran’s tutelage, Hezbollah had emerged as a force in Lebanese politics and a powerful adversary to Israel, whose 2006 invasion it repelled using a stock of rudimentary short-range rockets and Iranian-made drones. Along with Iran, it also offered support to Hamas, which did not yet control Gaza. The Houthis were at the time a small insurgency hiding out in caves in northern Yemen, still a few years away from receiving meaningful support from Tehran. Iranian and Hezbollah operatives had just begun training Iraqi Shiite groups fighting U.S. forces in Iraq, teaching them how to organize insurgent cells, use small arms such as AK-47s and rocket launchers, and build roadside bombs. In the decades since, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has developed a strategy for bringing these and other groups’ capabilities into the twenty-first century. Would-be axis members first receive basic training, both in Iran and, increasingly, territory controlled by other axis groups. Groups that prove themselves on the battlefield are given more advanced weapons, including one-way attack drones that are cruder than the Shahed-136s Iran itself uses but nonetheless able to strike targets far from their headquarters. Since at least 2025, for example, Tehran has provided Islamic Resistance in Iraq groups with a steady supply of the Shahed-101 and Shahed-107 drones used to target U.S. military bases and Gulf state infrastructure over the past six months. A small number of trusted groups are taught to build their own weapons, primarily drones, from parts they import themselves. Today, Hamas, Hezbollah, and the Houthis can all build and field their own one-way attack drones, firing them at targets up to 1,600 miles away. By carefully honing their organizational capabilities, the IRGC has transformed these groups from cell-based insurgents into highly capable organizations. Hamas, Hezbollah, and the Houthis have assembled their own rosters of smugglers, businesspeople, traders, and engineers to procure and build weaponry. Although these groups may appear to outsiders as only loosely intertwined, they have over time come to perform the functions of the military-industrial bases of rich, powerful states. Washington can no longer fall back on political pressure, sanctions, and military strikes. The IRGC has also subcontracted training to axis groups. Through this process, the groups have built direct connections to one another and to other powerful state and nonstate actors. In 2010, for example, all documented drone training for Hezbollah took place in Iran and was led by Iranian instructors. By 2015, Hezbollah had begun hosting training courses for other groups, such as Hamas, the Houthis, and Iraqi militias. According to a forthcoming Century International report, as of 2026, the Houthis were teaching the Somali al-Qaeda affiliate al-Shabab how to fly basic drones at training sites in Yemen, and, alongside IRGC operatives, may be tutoring Sudanese Islamist factions on how to build one-way attack drones at sites in Sudan. For a number of years, IRGC capacity building appeared to be paying off. Between 2011 and 2023, Hezbollah played a growing role in propping up the Iranian-allied Assad regime in Syria’s civil war, building a substantial footprint at military bases across the country alongside the IRGC and enjoying a constant flow of arms and other material support from Iran. Iranian-backed militias in Iraq helped push back the Islamic State (also known as ISIS) in Iraq and Syria and established a powerful presence within the Iraqi state security apparatus. The Houthis seized control of northwestern Yemen, and Hamas’s military and political grip on Gaza strengthened. Then came October 7. Hamas’s attack on Israel had enormous repercussions for Iran’s allies around the region, and, ultimately, Iran itself. Hamas was decimated, along with much of Gaza, by the Israeli response. In September 2024, Israel launched strikes on Beirut that killed Hezbollah’s secretary-general, Hassan Nasrallah, and much of the organization’s senior command. Later that year, as Iran and Hezbollah decreased their support and focused on their own survival, a rebel offensive caused the collapse of the Assad regime in Syria. Then, during the 12-day war in June 2025, the United States and Israel launched waves of attacks on Iran that leaders in both countries claimed had obliterated the Islamic Republic’s air defenses and its ability to launch missile and drone attacks. Months later, an Israeli strike killed a number of senior Houthi leaders in Yemen, including the top commander of the group’s drone and missile programs. Israeli officials, along with some U.S. officials, were confident that Iran and its regional allies were in terminal decline. Yet less than a year later, they appear to have reconstituted themselves. Iran launched a huge campaign of drone and missile strikes on Gulf infrastructure and U.S. military installations across the Middle East in response to Operation Epic Fury. Iraqi militias have launched hundreds of drone and missile strikes against U.S. military bases in Iraq and Jordan, along with waves of attacks on the Gulf states. Hezbollah has mounted a stiffer-than-anticipated defense of southern Lebanon after the Israeli ground invasion in March. And a year after the Houthis agreed to end targeting of American commercial ships—a move the Trump administration took as a sign the group had been defeated—they have resumed attacks on vessels passing through the Red Sea, imposing a de facto blockade on Saudi ports along the waterway. They have also targeted Saudi energy infrastructure for the first time since the UN-brokered truce brought the Yemeni civil war to a halt in 2022. SELF-ASSEMBLY LINE American and Israeli predictions of Iranian and axis defeat missed an important shift in the way the IRGC and its allies organize their military and organizational capabilities. Whereas military and technological know-how were once concentrated within the IRGC, they have since become embedded across a much more diffuse, interconnected ecosystem. Even in early 2025, after the setbacks in Gaza, Lebanon, and Syria, and after the Trump administration designated the Houthis a foreign terrorist organization, Iran and axis groups were able to quickly rebuild themselves and their arsenals by tapping into the diversified knowledge bases and supply lines they had developed over the last 15 years. The clearest evidence of that shift is in how several of Iran’s proxy groups now arm themselves. When, in 2024, we started investigating how Houthis arm themselves, American and European officials repeatedly told us that the main source of the group’s arsenal was weapons smuggled from Iran into Yemen on traditional wooden sailing vessels known as dhows. But by that point, the Houthis had already begun building their own weapons, using supply chains as complex as the local and global trade routes that crisscross the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean. American and Israeli officials had similarly assumed that most of Hezbollah’s arms came from Iran, and that the collapse of the Assad regime would cut off an important weapons supply line. But Hezbollah, like the Houthis, had built alternative supply chains. The 2024 arrest of a Hezbollah operative found to have been using a mass of shell companies in Spain and Germany to re-export drone parts to Lebanon should have sounded alarms in Washington and Israel that the group’s procurement structures were changing: months before the collapse of the Assad regime, the operative was attempting to transport as many as 2,000 engines—enough to reconstitute Hezbollah’s estimated pre-2023 drone fleet. Iran and its allies still smuggle the old-fashioned way, too. These new supply lines, in which parts travel separately across the globe and are assembled near the point of use, are also useful in neutralizing another important U.S. strategy for countering Iran and its proxies: sanctions and terrorism designations, which threaten punitive action against individuals suspected of working with designated groups. At the turn of this century, these tools were useful for combating arms proliferation because the United States and its allies controlled most of the exports, trade routes, and financial networks needed to buy and move arms and advanced manufactured goods. Until the mid-2010s, the United States and its allies were able to throttle Iran’s drone program by targeting individuals and companies suspected of supplying parts to Tehran. In 2009, for example, German authorities arrested a group of Iranian businessmen who were trying to ship drone engines to Iran by claiming they were Jet Ski engines. But Chinese manufacturers now produce the intermediate goods needed to build drones at increasing scale and shrinking cost. China does not restrict the sale of many of the parts used to make weaponized drones because, Beijing claims, they are made for civilian use. In many cases, it refuses to take its own punitive measures against Chinese firms that have been sanctioned by the United States for selling them for this reason. Today, Chinese and Iranian copies of those purported Jet Ski engines are powering the Russian and Iranian drone campaigns in Ukraine and the Middle East. Using Chinese commercial websites such as Alibaba, Iran and axis groups can build the Ababil-T, historically the workhorse drone of the axis fleet, from readily available Chinese-origin parts for about $1,500. All Hezbollah needs to obtain and retrofit the first-person drones it has been using to target the Israel Defense Forces since early 2026 is a credit card, access to YouTube instructional videos, and a bit of manufacturing acumen. The chokepoints that matter for drone proliferation are not under U.S. control. The sheer volume of global trade makes it nearly impossible for even well-resourced states to track these shipments from China. In most cases, parts are bought by anonymous shell companies, often registered in so-called secrecy jurisdictions—places where local laws allow companies to be incorporated without publicly disclosing their ownership structures—and transported in some of the five million to six million shipping containers that navigate the high seas daily. The containers are dropped off and collected at trade hubs that prioritize ease of doing business over screening cargo or sanctions compliance. When shell companies are sanctioned, their owners simply shut them down and register new ones. Iran and its allies still smuggle the old-fashioned way, too. Tehran has a long track record of shipping arms to allied groups by sea, both through smugglers in small boats and with its own fleet of container ships. More recently, it has worked with a tangle of dodgy international businessmen to build a “shadow fleet” of vessels even harder for Western authorities to track. For example, one network of cargo ships regularly switches off its on-board automatic identification systems in the Gulf of Oman before going on so-called dark runs to the Iranian port of Shahid Rajaee, turning the systems back on only after the ships have cleared the Strait of Hormuz. Many of these ships transported unidentified cargo to Syria before the collapse of the Assad regime and continue to carry shipments to Houthi-controlled ports in Yemen. The ships are connected, through shell companies, to a single Syrian businessman who has been repeatedly sanctioned for moving oil and money for Iran and Hezbollah. Iranian state-owned ships, meanwhile, have recently returned to the Mediterranean after avoiding the region between 2023 and 2025, docking regularly at Libyan ports. Israeli and Libyan researchers have concluded that Iranian materiel is now being transported from Libya to Tehran’s allies in Lebanon, Sudan, and potentially Gaza. And even under the new Shara government in Syria, which has pledged to prevent arms transfers, cross-border smuggling into Lebanon is still happening via Syrian roads and ports. Put together, these continually evolving supply lines and relationships have helped transform Iran’s network of regional allies into a complex and highly adaptive web of actors. DEAL WITH IT The new reality of the axis requires a new strategy. A more promising approach to blunting the threat posed by Iran and its allies must first acknowledge that relying on military force and economic warfare alone will only lead to repeated cycles of conflict that could drag the United States into yet another open-ended war in the Middle East. Washington should instead prioritize some combination of continued disruption of axis commercial and financial networks, splitting from the axis groups not yet fully embedded in the ecosystem, such as the groups in the Horn of Africa the Houthis are recruiting, and engaging politically with more established groups, particularly as they take on governance in the territory they hold. Deals would not necessarily resemble bilateral agreements like the U.S.-Houthi truce. Instead, they should take the form of structured agreements, aimed at brokering lasting country-level political settlements across the region, accompanied by U.S.-Iranian diplomacy. Alternatively, Washington could throw caution to the wind and adopt the IRGC’s playbook, building its own array of state and nonstate actors to fight against the axis on the United States’ behalf. But training groups to develop and use their own weapons would be an arduous undertaking, and it would come with serious risks. Given the United States’ spotty record building up allied states’ conventional forces and its tendency to discard state and nonstate allies as soon as they no longer serve Washington’s purposes, attempting to do so again could have catastrophic consequences. However it decides to deal with the axis, Washington will struggle to rein in the spread of advanced weapons that can be built from commercially available parts on its own. The United States may still be the world’s most advanced economy but the chokepoints that matter for drone proliferation are not under its control. China, for now, has little reason to help Washington curb purchases of drone parts by armed groups. But Beijing is worried about the threat drones pose to its own domestic security, and entrepôts such as the United Arab Emirates that have long looked the other way may be changing their own thinking after weathering waves of Shahed-136s earlier this year. A multilateral initiative to improve tracking of dual-use components and agreed-on penalties for their transfer to nonstate armed groups could constrain armed groups’ ability to build large drone arsenals in the future. The right approach will combine all these efforts, eschewing the sort of totalizing theory of the case that has failed in the past. What Washington cannot do is turn back time. Hoping for the collapse of Iran and its allies around the region will not be enough to destroy this still potent network. New ideas are needed. item.content:encoded: Security researchers say they have evidence that a Chinese-linked spyware has expanded from mainland China to now target victims in over a dozen countries, including across Europe and the United States. The previously identified spyware also has new functionality capable of stealing troves of data and remotely bricking devices. The researchers at cybersecurity firm Arctic Wolf said that the LightSpy spyware, first discovered in 2018 and previously linked to Chinese state-backed hackers, has since evolved into a commercial spyware platform operated by a single threat actor who caters to governments, enterprises, and militaries. The platform is said to feature custom branding, billing, and demos for advertising it to prospective customers. The findings underscore how the use of spyware continues to proliferate beyond governments and nation-backed hackers, and more broadly into the private industry. LightSpy is a modular spyware platform that allows whoever is controlling it to attack a multitude of different devices, including smartphones, Apple devices, Linux servers, and Windows PCs. By using exploits for each device, the spyware can steal large amounts of sensitive information from its targets, including precise location data, chat messages, screen recordings, and stored passwords. The researchers also said the code is capable of remotely wiping and destroying data on a compromised device. The researchers said that LightSpy has now been identified infecting routers, which researchers say they had not seen before. By attacking routers, the hackers can gain visibility and access to any other device on the same network. Some of the compromised routers are associated with NATO member countries, said Arctic Wolf. According to the company, LightSpy operates a network of at least 117 servers in several countries around the world. The researchers said they were able to link the latest activity to a Chinese contractor after one of the spyware’s operators used the LightSpy administrator’s panel to place an order with Kentucky Fried Chicken using his real name and office address.

item.content:encoded: China has started low-volume production of domestically developed immersion DUV lithography machines, with around five systems planned for this year and roughly 20 in 2027, according to a report from July 27, which wiped roughly $44 billion off ASML's market value. The manufacturer was named as Shanghai Aishengna Electronic Technology Group by Reuters the following day, a state-owned company established in August 2023 with 7 billion yuan (around $1 billion) in registered capital that absorbed engineering teams from Huawei-affiliated startup Yuliangsheng and state scanner maker SMEE. The first units are due at SMIC, Hua Hong, and CXMT this year for production-line validation rather than volume output, but the machines are far from matching ASML's models and still require further testing. Five machines represent about 3.8% of the roughly 130 immersion systems ASML deploys in a typical year (a class of lithography machines that put a super thin layer of liquid over the wafer during processing), with the European giant holding an estimated 98.7% of the total immersion market. The Chinese tool reportedly prints 28nm-class features in a single exposure and reaches 7nm, and theoretically 5nm, through multipatterning, the same route SMIC already runs on its installed ASML fleet. Neither company has confirmed the report, no machine has been shown publicly, and no throughput or overlay figures have been disclosed, against the 330 wafers per hour and 2.5nm overlay of ASML's current flagship immersion tools. SMIC’s scanner SMIC has been running a domestic immersion scanner, developed under the codename Mount Everest, since September last year, when the Financial Times reported that China's largest foundry had begun testing the Yuliangsheng tool with production-line integration targeted from 2027 after qualification. FT compared the machine against ASML's Twinscan NXT:1950i, a system that entered the market in 2008, which puts the design roughly a decade and a half behind the tools ASML sells today. Yuliangsheng, founded in Shanghai in 2022 with 1 billion yuan (around $149 million) in registered capital, is understood to have delivered three lithography machines to fabs for testing by late last year, but this hasn’t been officially confirmed. Many of the critical components needed for the machines are still imported from Japan, and delays at those local suppliers are what have capped 2026 output at around five units. The 2027 target of 20 machines is therefore an ambitious target that assumes a domestic component base that hasn't been established yet, and the imported parts remain within reach of any future export-control round. 18% litho localization SMEE's most advanced shipping product remains the SSA600 series, a 90nm-class dry ArF scanner that was in mass production as of May last year. The 28nm-capable SSA/800 immersion tool the company announced in 2023 has never been deployed, and a state-media claim of its successful development was deleted shortly after publication. In December last year, SMEE won a roughly RMB 110 million ($16 million) single-source government contract for a KrF scanner specified at 110nm resolution and 15nm overlay, a useful indicator of where its production-grade capability is at the moment. Domestic equipment took 35% of Chinese fab purchases in 2025, beating Beijing's 30% target and up from about 10% three years earlier, according to figures from China's semiconductor industry association. Etch and thin-film deposition passed 40% localization, and metrology reached 25%, while lithography managed just 18%, most of it in trailing-edge and packaging tools. From the end of 2025, new fab capacity additions are required to source at least half their equipment domestically, a mandate that guarantees the new scanners a customer base, whatever their specs turn out to be. Etch, deposition, and everything else Naura Technology became the world's fifth-largest chip equipment maker by 2025 sales, trailing only ASML, Applied Materials, Lam Research, and Tokyo Electron, and moving ahead of KLA. The company booked RMB 27.14 billion ($4 billion USD) in revenue in the first three quarters of 2025 against RMB 6.05 billion ($589 million USD) for all of 2020, holds an order backlog stretching into 2027, and has started developing lithography tools for the first time. AMEC grew revenue and net profit by more than 30% in 2025, while cleaning specialist ACM Research posted $901.3 million for fiscal 2025 and guided to as much as $1.18 billion for 2026. SiCarrier, the Shenzhen firm widely linked to Huawei, debuted around 30 tools at SEMICON China in March 2025, spanning etch, deposition, metrology, and test, and was reportedly valued at RMB 65 billion ($9.63 billion USD) by September 2025 with more than RMB 10 billion ($1.48 billion USD) in orders. The U.S. added it to the Entity List in December 2024. The sector's own leadership is less triumphant than the numbers suggest. In March, SMIC co-founder Wang Yangyuan and the heads of YMTC, Naura, and EDA firm Empyrean jointly described China's tool industry as "small, fragmented, and weak" and called for national consolidation, with Big Fund III's $47.5 billion being redirected toward lithography and EDA. The Aishengna venture, which merged the Yuliangsheng and SMEE teams into one state-owned vehicle, looks like the first product of that pressure to consolidate. China spent a record $49.5 billion on wafer fab equipment in 2024, per SEMI, and remains the world's largest buyer through 2027, even after a pullback in 2025. EUV lithography A Reuters investigation in December 2025, dubbed China’s “Manhattan Project,” described an operational prototype EUV light-source machine in a high-security Shenzhen lab, completed in early 2025, that generates EUV photons but hasn't yet exposed a wafer. More than 3,000 researchers are said to work across the program, with Huawei playing the coordinating role and SMEE handling system integration. Two teams are chasing the light source: one led by Lin Nan, a Beihang University professor who worked at ASML from 2015 to 2021, has a solid-state laser-produced-plasma design running at 3.42% conversion efficiency against the roughly 5.5% commercial viability required, while Zhao Yongpeng's laser-assisted discharge plasma group at Harbin Institute of Technology has reached around 100W of EUV output against the roughly 600W that ASML's production sources deliver. Beijing's target is chip output from the machine by 2028, with Reuters' sources calling 2030 more realistic. A separate strand of reporting described a reverse-engineered prototype built around an intercepted Cymer light source that has likewise produced nothing. Earlier claims of a Huawei EUV trial production in 2025 and mass production in 2026, which circulated via Chinese media in March 2025, were never confirmed by any primary source. Tsinghua University's accelerator-based SSMB concept, which would need a synchrotron of a staggering 100 to 150 meters in circumference, remains an academic project. Export controls The MATCH Act, introduced in the House and Senate in early April, would ban not only sales of immersion DUV tools to SMIC, Huawei, Hua Hong, CXMT, and YMTC but also the servicing of machines already installed, and would give the Netherlands and Japan 150 days to align. At this stage, it remains a bill, not a law, but servicing restrictions would strike directly at the installed ASML base that produces every advanced chip China currently makes, including SMIC's N+3 node in Huawei's Kirin 9030. Chinese fabs have been preparing for exactly that scenario by using third-party engineers and gray-market parts to Frankenstein older ASML machines. ASML's China exposure is already shrinking on schedule, with the country representing 20% of system sales compared to 41% in 2024 and 33% last year, even as the company raised full-year guidance to €43 to €45 billion in July. Likewise, Applied Materials expects to lose $600 to $710 million in China revenue this fiscal year. Ultimately, three markers will indicate whether China’s domestic DUV program is a legitimate rival or yet more state-sanctioned hot air. The main one would be validated production wafers from an Aishengna tool at SMIC, Hua Hong, or CXMT with published throughput and yield, followed by delivery of anything close to the 20 machines planned for 2027, and a first exposed wafer from the Shenzhen EUV prototype before the 2028 target set by Beijing. Luke James is a freelance writer and journalist. Although his background is in legal, he has a personal interest in all things tech, especially hardware and microelectronics, and anything regulatory.

item.title: The War China Might Choose
item.description: Score: 5.62 The article analyzes potential military coercion options China might use against Taiwan, comparing a traditional blockade, a joint firepower strike, and a novel 'blockade by fire' targeting port infrastructure. item.content:encoded: Analysts generally organize the options for a Chinese military move against Taiwan into three categories: an invasion to seize direct control of the island; a “joint firepower strike” that would bomb Taiwan’s cities and political institutions, terrorizing Taiwanese civilians into surrender; and a maritime blockade to starve Taiwan into submission. All these missions are complex, high-cost gambles for China that would consume large quantities of military assets and result in immense casualties and property damage. A blockade would add the risk of directly attacking third parties—specifically, cargo ships from other countries—making it more likely that China would also have to fight international powers, including the United States. Nevertheless, many analysts think that a blockade is the most tempting scenario of the three for Beijing, because it would avoid sending Chinese forces up against Taiwan’s prepared defenses and would capitalize on what Chinese leaders consider Taiwan’s vulnerabilities, including the island’s extreme dependence on international trade. Still, a traditional blockade risks escalation and imposes extensive military costs on China. But China has an underexamined option, one that could generate the effects of a traditional blockade with a lower cost for Beijing. A “blockade by fire”—a missile strike campaign directed specifically against Taiwan’s port infrastructure—would minimize the risks that China would face. This kind of strike would not focus major combat operations in the heart of Taiwan’s cities, as in the case of an invasion or a joint firepower strike. Nor would it put third-party ships at risk, as with a traditional blockade. And because a blockade by fire would use only a small number of missiles aimed at a narrow set of targets in Taiwanese ports, it would avoid the need to enforce a cordon around the island and would not expose China’s navy to defensive missile fire from Taiwan. Under a blockade by fire, international commercial ships would still be free to sail around the island, meaning that other East Asian countries such as Japan and South Korea could continue the bulk of their trade essentially undisturbed. Ships could even sail to Taiwan, but they would be unable to load and unload cargo in the heavily damaged ports. Simulation models of attacks like this suggest that China could substantially interrupt Taiwan’s trade and keep it suppressed for an extended period, using only a few hundred ballistic missiles. Global trade would have to adjust to any type of blockade against Taiwan. In fact, the indirect economic pain to other countries from a blockade by fire would be the same as that of a traditional blockade scenario. The key difference is that a blockade by fire would not involve direct Chinese attacks on non-Taiwanese ships. The destruction would be limited to Taiwanese assets, helping Beijing maintain its argument that the operation was strictly an internal matter and ensuring that international powers couldn’t claim a greater need to intervene. Overall, a blockade by fire would make efficient use of China’s military assets. Given the limited number of targets, the Chinese military would be able to reserve the bulk of its capabilities, including the majority of its missile arsenal, to deter the United States and other countries from coming to Taiwan’s aid. Intervention is always possible, but a blockade by fire minimizes this risk compared to alternatives. Taiwan, and its international partners, should prepare for such a strategy. Investing in responses to China’s traditional threats is important, but will not be enough. The island should prepare its ports and its people for the supply disruptions of a potential blockade by fire. BLOCK AID Any move that Beijing may make against Taiwan, traditional blockade or otherwise, is fraught with risk. If they decide on conflict, Chinese leaders have strong incentives to find military strategies that minimize backlash, and although a traditional blockade is seen as less escalatory than an invasion, it still presents challenges for Beijing. To enforce a traditional blockade, China would likely need to fire its weapons. Although China’s maritime militia fleet regularly harasses other countries’ small and vulnerable fishing boats, the container ships and bulk carriers responsible for Taiwan’s commerce dwarf any Chinese militia vessel. Giant cargo carriers would have little reason to comply with Chinese requests to divert their course. Mariners follow the “law of gross tonnage”: small ships give way. In fact, it is in their interest to do so, because the hulking commercial ships will hardly notice them in a collision. Just as the U.S. Navy was forced to open fire periodically to maintain its blockade against Iran, China would likely have to fire on any determined ships headed for Taiwanese ports in order to actually stop them. China would thus have the last clear chance to back down from all-out warfare. As the American economist Thomas Schelling argued decades ago, the country with the final opportunity to avoid escalation often loses in a crisis. In attempting a traditional blockade, China would have already chosen to fight a war against Taiwan. Any blockade is by definition an act of war. But the actions necessary to enforce a traditional blockade risk expanding the war beyond Taiwan, because the threats against non-Taiwanese vessels would not only pressure the United States and others to intervene to protect their shipping but also give them discrete targets against which to retaliate. It is easier for outside powers, notably the United States, to intervene against a traditional blockade than against other military coercion because they could do so in a limited way, focusing only on China’s aggressor ships. The intervenors could do this even if they would be unwilling to escalate to direct strikes against the Chinese mainland. Thus, a traditional blockade would inevitably create a hot conflict, and one that makes it relatively easy for China’s opponents to respond. To enforce a traditional blockade, China would likely need to fire its weapons. A blockade by fire, however, would accomplish the goal of a traditional blockade without these drawbacks. In our research, we ran a series of simulations that modeled Taiwanese port operations, how Chinese missile attacks might inhibit them, and what Taiwan might do to defend them. The results suggest that China would need to fire fewer than 500 missiles over 100 days to reduce Taiwan’s imports to 15 percent of their average peacetime level. Beijing would not need to actively track and intercept commercial ships traveling to Taiwan, making direct confrontation with outside powers less likely. China could also be confident that few international ships would be accidentally hit while docked and that few missiles would land outside Taiwan’s ports, where they could hurt civilians. For all these reasons, a blockade by fire might be more acceptable to Chinese leaders than other military options against Taiwan. Although a blockade by fire involves a missile strike campaign, it is not simply an alternative form of joint firepower strike. The key difference is the type of target being attacked. Under a blockade by fire, as with a traditional blockade, the damage to Taiwan occurs through increasing supply shortages and rising prices, not conflagrations in Taiwan’s major cities. A blockade of any type would give Taiwan the chance to acquiesce before it suffered high costs. Unlike a firepower strike’s irreversibility—destroyed buildings, decapitated government institutions, and dead civilians—a blockade by fire would allow Taiwan’s people and leaders to see the suffering coming before it fully hit. China might even promise to rapidly bring aid to Taiwan if it agrees to Beijing’s stipulations, providing further incentive for Taiwan to capitulate quickly. ADAPT AND SURVIVE To deter a blockade by fire, Taiwan’s most obvious move would be to bulk up its missile defenses. But while some missile defense is surely a component of Taiwan’s best response, making it the centerpiece would be a losing strategy. Modern missile defense systems are increasingly effective, but they are also enormously expensive. Each interceptor missile costs somewhat more than each ballistic missile that it is designed to intercept, and the defending force often needs to fire more than one interceptor at each incoming missile to create a high chance of interception. Taiwan would wind up on the losing side of a spending race with China over short-range ballistic missiles. And even if the United States were to support Taiwanese defense efforts, the two would still struggle to keep up with Chinese capabilities. Taiwan would similarly struggle if it tried to deter a blockade by fire by threatening China’s ports with reciprocal short-range ballistic missile strikes. Unlike Taiwan, China has many domestic resources to draw on, land borders across which it can bring imports even if its seaborne trade is disrupted, and ports that are out of Taiwan’s missile range. Any Chinese threat to hurt Taiwan therefore outpaces what Taiwan could threaten in response. Taiwan’s allies could attack Chinese ports that are out of Taiwan’s range, but that would be a dramatic escalation against a nuclear-armed power and would still not address China’s resources advantage. Taiwan’s best hope, then, for deterring and defending itself from a blockade by fire would be to prepare to survive one. Taiwan should stockpile essential items, including the parts and materials needed to repair port infrastructure. Taiwan and its willing partners should also conduct exercises that specifically focus on preparing the island’s ports to operate under crisis conditions and to practice mitigating and repairing damage. These exercises should take cues from other countries that have faced aerial attacks on their port infrastructure, such as Germany and the United Kingdom in World War II, North Vietnam during the Vietnam War, and Ukraine in its war with Russia. Taiwan and its partners could also build or subsidize a reserve of roll-on, roll-off cargo vessels—ships with built-in ramps that allow wheeled vehicles to drive cargo directly between the vessel and the port. These ships can continue to load and unload even without the dedicated port infrastructure, such as cranes, that is needed for modern container shipping. Although these vessels are less efficient than container ships and bulk carriers, they could play a valuable role in getting essential supplies into Taiwan in the case of a blockade by fire. OUTSIDE THE BOX Ultimately, the greatest inhibitor of a Chinese blockade by fire is that blockades of any kind are hard. Historical experience—including during both world wars, Cuba’s long history under U.S. embargo, and more contemporary conflicts in Ukraine and the Red Sea—suggests that target economies adjust. They find ways to trade in spite of blockades, and they draw on domestic resources that they would not use in normal times but that can help under duress. These adjustments add to the fact that while blockades can impose privation, modern governments and their nationalist populations can accept a lot of suffering before considering major political concessions. Even absent Chinese aggression, people in Taiwan increasingly identify as Taiwanese and do not seem inclined to repeat Hong Kong’s experience of acquiescing to Chinese rule. Most Taiwanese prefer the status quo, and a Chinese military move might compound Taiwanese resistance by stirring a nationalist backlash. Nevertheless, Chinese leaders are subject to their own political pressures, and they may view China’s military buildup and modernization optimistically. Leaders who come to believe they can succeed with an attack, whether through innovation or perceived military might, sometimes decide to go for it. Or they may fatalistically roll the dice in a moment of stress. Because a blockade by fire lowers the military and political risks inherent in taking action against Taiwan, there is a strong possibility that Beijing would reach for this option if Chinese leaders deemed military action necessary. Taiwan of course needs traditional defenses. Notably, a robust force of mobile land-based antiship and surface-to-air missiles would help Taiwan against both a Chinese invasion and a traditional blockade. But analysts also need to expand their vision of creative strategies that China could use to coerce Taiwan. To maintain deterrence against a blockade by fire, Taiwan and those hoping to help it need to first acknowledge such an option and then dynamically adapt the island’s defenses to deter and survive this alternative approach.
